title: Trump says US no longer needs Iran deal as Houthis claim strikes on Saudi oil routes
dek: Brent crude climbed back towards $96 after attack claims on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea oil outlet and on tankers in Hormuz. India, which imports most of its oil, is exposed on prices and shipping.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, as Yemen's Houthis claimed drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia's main oil export routes and Iranian forces claimed explosions on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude, which had fallen to about $91 a barrel early on Thursday, was trading near $95.6 on Friday morning.

The flare-up follows signals from Mr Trump, after his party's heavy losses in the US midterm elections, that he did not intend to resume full-scale hostilities with Iran. On Thursday he said he would "not hesitate" to strike again if Tehran threatened US allies or shipping in the strait, while also saying he was holding back at the request of Gulf governments.

## What happened

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday, Mr Trump wrote: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." He added: "We've got their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we've got their strait."

In a radio interview the same day, asked what would happen if Iran killed a senior US official, he said Iran would not exist for long afterwards; reports differ slightly on his exact words. In a separate interview he said the US could "cripple" Iran's energy facilities, bridges and manufacturing "in three days", but that Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain had asked him to hold off. "I am not sure I agree with it," he said.

The Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said on Thursday that the group had hit a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, the oil installation at Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and an Aramco facility in Riyadh, according to reports. The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two Houthi drones, one over Riyadh and one over the Eastern Province. Saudi civil defence said air defences had destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Mecca, with debris falling on a village, according to reports. Neither Saudi Aramco nor the Saudi government had reported any damage to oil facilities by Friday evening India time, and the Houthi claims could not be independently verified.

At sea, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed explosions had struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after the vessels ignored warnings. Reports differ on how many: one says two supertankers carrying more than 4 million barrels between them, another says four tankers. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, which monitors shipping in the region, reported that a tanker had been hit by a projectile; reports differ on whether anyone on board was hurt.

## Background

The war began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran. A ceasefire followed in April, and a US-Iran navigation memorandum was signed in June, but reports said it had collapsed by August. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for a large share of the world's seaborne oil and liquefied natural gas, largely closed, and the US has enforced what Iran's president calls a naval blockade.

Because of the closure, Saudi Arabia has been sending much of its crude west across the kingdom through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu, which is why Houthi attacks on that route matter well beyond Yemen. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed this year after the UN-brokered truce of 2022 broke down.

The Ministry of External Affairs said on 3 November that 23 Indians, 15 of them seafarers, had been killed since the war began.

## What Tehran says

Speaking alongside Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye on Thursday, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Israel had "played the role of a fire-starter" and, "by deceiving Trump, has pushed him toward war", according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. He said Iran "will not surrender".

Iran's Assembly of Experts, the clerical body that oversees the Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, called for a review of Iran's membership of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and a revision of its defence doctrine, according to reports. It did not say Iran would leave the treaty. Mohsen Rezaei, a senior security official, said on Wednesday that not a "single particle" of enriched nuclear material would leave Iran, and warned of consequences if the US struck again, according to reports.

In Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leads a caretaker government after his bloc lost its majority in October's election, one television report said military chiefs had told him there was no immediate need to strike Iran but that Israel should join if Mr Trump renewed attacks. Another report said intelligence Mr Netanyahu had presented supported his case for resuming the fight. The two accounts could not be reconciled.

## Why it matters for India

India imports most of the crude oil it uses, and the war has already reshaped its economy. October retail inflation was 6.09%, above the Reserve Bank's upper limit, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi said this week that the government had absorbed Rs 43 a litre of diesel costs to shield farmers. The rupee closed at 94.24 to the dollar on Friday, 21 paise weaker on the day, according to market reports, and Indian shares fell, with traders citing oil and inflation.

The attacks on the Yanbu route are a particular risk: with Hormuz shut, Saudi Red Sea exports are one of the few large sources of Gulf crude still reaching Asian buyers. Thousands of Indian seafarers also work on ships in the region. At the MEA's weekly briefing on Friday, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the well-being and safety of Indian seafarers were "of high importance" to the government.

## What happens next

Mr Trump has not set out conditions for new strikes beyond threats to allies and shipping. Oil traders were watching for any confirmed damage to Saudi facilities: Brent was still on course for a second weekly fall of more than 2.5%, according to reports, after a sharp drop the week before as hopes of de-escalation grew.

## Key numbers

- Brent crude: about $95.6 a barrel on Friday morning, up from about $91.3 early on Thursday
- 23 Indians killed since 28 February, 15 of them seafarers (MEA, 3 November)
- Rupee: 94.24 to the dollar at Friday's close
